summary: A survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers from August 1974, showing how far sites had come in implementing the new Telnet protocol. It is a status snapshot. It is updated by RFC 702.

eli5.summary: This is a progress check from August 1974 on which computers had built the new Telnet.

questions: which hosts supported new telnet in 1974
subtitle: The first monthly check on which ARPANET hosts had built the new Telnet protocol.

tldr.problem: A new Telnet protocol was being rolled out, and nobody had an overview of which server hosts actually supported it.
tldr.mechanism: D. W. Dodds ran a surveying program from the new-protocol user Telnet at BBNA, added a few manual checks, and tabulated what each of 32 server hosts did as of 15 August 1974.
tldr.outcome: Fewer than one third of the server sites had any new-protocol server running, a month after the release of TENEX 1.32. RFC 702 updates this report.

today: RFC 701 is a snapshot from August 1974 and was updated by RFC 702. The RFC index lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Purpose of the Survey
sections.content:
RFC 701 is the first of what were planned to be monthly reports on the status of new-protocol Telnet implementations on server hosts of the ARPA network. It covers only server Telnets. The author hopes that any site with a working new-protocol server also has a new-protocol user Telnet, and says this can be assumed for TENEX sites running TENEX 1.32. No further claims are made.

The author is sorry to report that, a month after the release of TENEX 1.32, less than one third of the server sites had any new-protocol server operating.
sections.eli5: This is the first of a planned series of progress checks on the new Telnet. Not many computers were ready yet.

sections.title: The Summary Counts
sections.content:
Of 32 server hosts, 10 (31%) had a new-protocol implementation, 19 (59%) had none and 3 (9%) were of unknown status because they were down to the network. Of the 10, 5 ran the new protocol on socket 27 with the old one on socket 1, 4 ran it on both socket 1 and socket 27, and 1 ran it on socket 1 only.

Only half of the sites with a new-protocol server were using the logger socket conventions correctly, as the author understood them. The sites in the first group (new on socket 27, old on socket 1) are the ones whose operation is 100% correct by the author's reading.
sections.eli5: Out of 32 computers, about 10 had the new tool, 19 did not, and 3 could not be reached at all.

sections.title: The Tabulation and Options
sections.content:
A table lists each server host by number and name, what it offers on socket 1 and socket 27 (OLD, NEW, X for no server, or ? for unknown) and which options it implements. I# means option number # is implemented incoming to the user (the server says WILL #). O# means outgoing from the user (the server says DO #).

The options implemented by anyone are 0 Transmit-Binary, 1 Echo, 3 Suppress-Go-Ahead and 6 Timing-Mark. A note says SU-AI seems to send an improper response to a request for option 0.
sections.eli5: The table is a checklist. Each computer gets a row, and the columns show which new features it can do.

sections.title: Caveats
sections.content:
All data came from a survey program run at various times plus a few manual checks. It shows how servers behave as seen by the new-protocol user Telnet at BBNA on 15 August 1974, and other sites' surveys may differ. The report was submitted on 20 August 1974.

Some servers listed as new-protocol on socket 1 actually try to talk to both old and new user Telnets, depending on which control sequences they receive.
sections.eli5: The author warns that the results come from one place on one day, so other people might see slightly different answers.
